title: FRM Credit Risk, Lesson 1: The Credit Default Swap (CDS) - mechanics and basic pricing
subtitle: Buying insurance on a debt you do not even need to hold the bond for
whyItMatters: The CDS is the most widely used credit derivative and also the central character of the 2008 crisis (AIG sold CDS without holding enough capital against them). Understanding how a CDS works is the precondition for understanding both how credit risk is hedged and how that risk can travel far beyond the balance sheet of the bank where it started.
openingQuestion: In a Credit Default Swap (CDS) contract, what does the protection buyer do?
openingOptions: Pays a periodic fee in exchange for compensation if the borrower defaults
Lends money directly to the reference entity at a fixed interest rate
Buys shares in the reference entity to hedge against price risk
Receives a periodic fee and bears the risk if the reference entity defaults
explanation: A CDS works like an insurance contract: the protection buyer pays a fee (the CDS spread, quoted in basis points per year on the notional) steadily to the protection seller. If a credit event occurs at the reference entity - default, or a debt restructuring - the seller has to compensate the buyer. Unlike direct lending, neither side needs any credit relationship with the reference entity at all, and that is precisely why a CDS can be used to speculate rather than only to hedge.

diagram.label: The protection buyer pays a periodic fee (the CDS spread)
The protection seller takes the fee and promises to pay on a credit event
The seller compensates by the loss rate (1 − recovery rate)

realWorldExample.description: AIG Financial Products sold an enormous volume of CDS protection on CDOs tied to subprime debt, collecting fees steadily for years while setting aside almost no capital against a scenario of mass default. When the US housing market collapsed, AIG had to pay out on a great many contracts at once, producing losses that forced a $182 billion US government rescue - because AIG, though not a bank, had become a link in systemic risk through the CDS market.

quiz.question: What does the CDS spread tell you about the reference entity?
options: The interest rate that entity currently pays on customer deposits
A higher market-assessed default probability means a wider CDS spread
The current share price of the reference entity on the exchange
The number of CDS contracts outstanding, which is unrelated to credit risk
quiz.explanation: The CDS spread is a near real-time market measure of credit risk: it widens quickly when the market worries about an entity's ability to repay, because a protection seller has to be paid more to accept a higher chance of paying out. A deposit rate is a funding cost, not a default probability. A share price moves for many reasons other than credit, including earnings and sentiment. And open interest measures how much trading has happened, not how risky the borrower is. The spread typically reacts faster than an official credit rating, because it does not wait for an agency to review anything.

quiz.question: Why can a CDS be used to speculate rather than only to hedge?
options: Because the law in every country requires CDS to be used for speculation
Because CDS trade only on a tightly supervised centralised exchange, never over the counter
The buyer need not own the reference entity's debt - a naked CDS is a pure bet
Because the CDS fee is fixed for the whole life of the contract, ignoring risk
quiz.explanation: Unlike ordinary property insurance, which requires you to demonstrate an insurable interest, a CDS lets you buy protection without holding the underlying debt at all. No law mandates speculation, and CDS have historically traded over the counter rather than only on exchange, which is part of why the exposures were hard to see. The spread is also not fixed: it is quoted afresh in the market every day. The naked CDS is a pure speculative instrument, and it became a major point of contention after 2008 because it lets the notional at risk grow far beyond the amount of debt that actually exists.

quiz.question: In the AIG episode of 2008, what was the core risk management failure?
options: The US government had banned AIG from the CDS market before the crisis hit
AIG took no part at all in credit derivatives before the 2008 crisis broke out
AIG only bought CDS to hedge and never sold protection to anyone else
AIG sold CDS and collected fees for years without reserving enough capital against them
quiz.explanation: This connects directly to model risk and enterprise risk management from earlier lessons: a steady stream of incoming fees creates a false sense of safety, while tail risk - many credit events firing at once in a systemic crisis - is mispriced and left without matching capital. AIG was not banned from the market, was very much active in credit derivatives, and was a net seller rather than a buyer of protection. The failure was not the instrument itself but the capital held against a correlated payout scenario.

quiz.question: What happens to the protection seller when the reference entity suffers a credit event?
options: The seller pays the buyer the loss: par minus whatever is recovered on the defaulted debt
The CDS contract simply terminates with no payment due from either side
The buyer owes the seller a penalty fee for having caused the credit event
Both sides are refunded every premium paid over the entire life of the contract
quiz.explanation: The payout equals par minus the recovery rate - if a defaulted bond still returns 40% of its value through bankruptcy proceedings, the seller pays only 60% of notional rather than the whole amount. The contract does not lapse without payment; that would defeat the entire purpose of buying protection. The buyer causes nothing, since the credit event belongs to a third party. And past premiums are the seller's earned compensation for having carried the risk, so they are never returned.

quiz.question: A reference bond has a notional of 10bn dong; after the credit event, 40% of par is recovered. How much must the protection seller pay?
options: 4bn dong (= 10 × 40%, taking the recovered portion by mistake)
6bn dong (= 10 × (1 − 40%), the actual loss)
10bn dong (= the full notional, ignoring the recovery)
3.6bn dong (= 6 × 60%, deducting the recovery rate twice)
quiz.explanation: The payout equals the real loss: notional minus recovered value, so 10 − 4 = 6bn. The recovery rate therefore drives the amount the seller pays directly - and it can only be determined after the credit event has happened. On the day the contract is signed, nobody knows what that number will be.

practicePrompt.question: A company's 5-year CDS jumps from 120 to 640 basis points in two weeks while its credit rating stays at BBB. How do you read that?
options: The market repriced the risk before the rating agency could catch up
The BBB rating is right, so 640 basis points is a temporary distortion
The two numbers measure different things and cannot be compared at all
The CDS widened because liquidity worsened, not because of credit risk
practicePrompt.explanation: A CDS spread is a PRICE - it has buyers and sellers putting real money behind it every day, so it updates continuously. A credit rating is an OPINION, reviewed on a cycle and often changed only once the information is already clear. A gap between the two is therefore normal, and it almost always leans the same way: the CDS moves first. 640 basis points means the market is demanding 6.4% a year to protect this debt, a level incompatible with BBB - and that is a signal worth acting on, not a distortion waiting to correct itself.

keyTakeaways: A CDS is a credit protection contract: the buyer pays a periodic fee, the seller compensates if a credit event hits the reference entity
The CDS spread reflects the market's assessment of default probability - it reacts fast, usually faster than an official credit rating
A naked CDS requires no ownership of the underlying debt, turning the CDS into a pure speculative instrument and amplifying systemic risk
AIG (2008): years of steady CDS fee income without enough capital reserved for many credit events landing at the same time

summary.keyIdea: The CDS spread is the market's assessment of default probability, and it reacts faster than a credit rating because it is a price rather than an opinion.
summary.commonMistake: Assuming the protection seller can always pay. AIG collected fees steadily for years without reserving enough capital for many simultaneous credit events.

application.title: Read the CDS as a signal
application.message: When an entity's CDS spread widens while its rating has not moved, the market is saying something the rating agency has not said yet.

sections.text: The CDS is often assumed to be complicated, but the core mechanism is as simple as an insurance policy: pay a fee regularly, receive compensation if the bad thing happens. The complicated part - and the dangerous part - is who is allowed to buy that insurance without owning the thing being insured.

sections.title: The components of a CDS contract
sections.subtitle: Four elements that define every contract

concepts.def: The debt issuer the CDS contract protects against - a company, a bank, or a government.
The condition that triggers payment - usually default, debt restructuring, or insolvency, defined by ISDA's standard terms.
The fee the buyer pays the seller, quoted in basis points per year on the notional - a real-time measure of credit risk.
The percentage of par recovered after default through bankruptcy proceedings - it determines the actual payout (1 − recovery rate).

sections.label: The naked CDS - the most contested point
sections.text: After the 2008 crisis, a number of European legislators proposed banning naked CDS on sovereign debt, worried that it creates an incentive to bet on a country's collapse. It is a demonstration that a legitimate hedging tool (buying a CDS to protect debt you actually hold) and a purely speculative one (buying a CDS while owning nothing) share the same technical mechanism, yet carry completely different implications for systemic risk.

lines: A CDS moves credit risk from where it originates to whoever is willing to accept it - but it does not remove the risk, it only relocates it, sometimes to a place without the capital to carry it.
Next lesson: what happens when hundreds of loans are pooled and sliced into different layers of risk - securitisation and CDO structures.

sections.title: Putting numbers into the CDS spread
sections.equation: Annual CDS spread ≈ Probability of default × (1 − Recovery rate)

example.title: Reading the default probability back out of the market price
example.calculation: A five-year CDS trading at 240 basis points, i.e. 2.4% a year · assumed recovery rate 40%
example.explanation: Insuring VND 100bn of debt costs VND 2.4bn a year. That price already contains a forecast: the market is pricing roughly a 4% chance of default per year. Change the recovery assumption from 40% to 20% and the implied probability falls to 3.0% - same spread, different conclusion, which is why the recovery rate has to be stated rather than left implicit.
